# Filename Parsing & Bulk Rename Utility

> ⚠️ **PARTIAL as of 2026-08-08.** Parsing and the audit shipped — `FileNameParser`, `MediaTitleParser`, `SeriesNameAudit`, `FileNameAuditView`.
> 
> **Still open:** [#17](https://github.com/mranlett/ViLM/issues/17) — per-content-class naming conventions and the library migration. That is the bulk-rename half of this spec and it is unbuilt.
> ✅ **Approved by the Human Operator, 2026-08-06.** Implementation may proceed (Constitution Art. II). Rewritten 2026-08-05 as a spec DERIVED from *The Library Graph*; the rewrite changes how the parser decides, not what it decides about, and much of Phase 1 was already built under the previous approval.
> 
> **Open questions resolved 2026-08-06** — see the resolution notes inline, each pointing at where the answer actually lives.
**Parent:** *The Library Graph* (Epic, Approved). **This spec owns two directions of one relationship:** reading metadata **out of** filenames into the graph, and generating filenames **from** the graph.
## ⚠️ The ordering is still the whole point
The original proposal was to rename files from the metadata already held. **Measured against the real library, that would have destroyed data.**
| Measure, drive library | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Assets | 2,101 |
| Assets with **no actor tag** in the catalogue | **1,172 (56%)** |
| …whose **filename encodes performers anyway** | **1,154** |
**For this library the filename is the richer record.** Renaming from the catalogue first would overwrite descriptive names with sparse ones and lose the only copy of that information.
**Human Operator:** *"Your approach of reading the file name into the catalogue is the right move regardless, because my one instance of a more mature collection of metadata won't be the universal standard."*
⚠️ **Measurement caveat, retained.** Every figure here is from the **drive** library. The iPhone library is 100% actor-tagged and the two must never be conflated — an error already made once, in the studio-disambiguation analysis.
## Phase 1 — Parse filenames into the graph
### D1 — The parser proposes; it never writes silently
Same contract as enrichment: produce a **reviewable diff**, apply on confirmation. A parser that wrote directly would be a bulk mutation of the whole library driven by a regex. A parsed value fills a blank; it never overwrites a curated one.
### D2 — ⭐ AMENDED: the lexicon decides when it exists; position decides when it does not
**Human Operator, 2026-08-05:** *"This system prioritizes studios (which we have a lexicon of downloaded and verified studio names) as folder and actors (which we have a lexicon of validated and matched actor names in our library). These validated lists should be data sources in our renamer and parser."*
The previous version resolved **position first, vocabulary second**, reasoned explicitly from *"a new or un-curated library has neither vocabulary"* — without which the parser would work best on the libraries that least need it.
⚠️ **CORRECTION, 2026-08-05, from reading the code.** D2 described position-first as though it were the implementation. **It never was.** `FileNameParser.parse` has always checked vocabulary first and used position only as a tie-breaker for segments vocabulary could not place. The spec and the code have disagreed since this was written.
What genuinely changed in Phase C is narrower and more useful: **validated names now outrank merely-present ones.** Previously every string in the library carried equal authority, so a token that was a confirmed studio *and* sat in the actor list — because an earlier parse guessed it there — resolved as an actor purely because actors are checked first. **Order was deciding what confidence should.**
**The generality reasoning is still correct and is not what changes.** The amendment:
| Situation | Primary signal |
| --- | --- |
| A validated lexicon exists and the token resolves to a node | **the lexicon decides** |
| No lexicon, or the token resolves to nothing | **position decides** — first = performers, last = studio, exactly as before |
A node is **validated** when it carries a confirmed external identity (Epic D5).
### When a token resolves to more than one node type
A name can be both a performer and a studio. Resolution order:
|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | If exactly one candidate node's type suits the token's **position**, take it |  |
| 2 | If several suit, or the best-suited contradicts position | **skip and report** — never pick by node count, recency or alphabetical order |
| 3 | If none suits position | **skip and report** |
⚠️ **A tie is never broken silently.** Every mechanical tie-break available here (most videos, most recently matched) encodes a bias the operator never agreed to, and the cost of guessing wrong is a video credited to the wrong person.
### Segment counts outside the grammar
| Segments | Reading |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **unparseable** — no separator, nothing to position. Reported, never guessed at |
| **2** | first = performers, last = studio |
| 3 | position + corpus/lexicon per the rules above |
| 4 | the full grammar |
| **5+** | **unparseable** — more segments than the grammar has fields; reported |
Measured share: 1 or 5 segments together account for **30 of 2,101 files (1%)**.
### Detecting truncation rather than absence
A generated name at or near the 250-character ceiling has probably had fields **dropped**, and the parser must not read that as the record lacking them.
**Rule:** if the base name length is within one field-width of the ceiling, trailing fields absent from the name are marked `possiblyTruncated` and produce **no proposal at all** — neither a fill nor a conflict. Below that length, absence is treated as genuine. This is what makes P1 verifiable. The generality argument survives intact — a day-one library still parses by position — while this library uses what it has confirmed.
### D3 — ⭐ NEW: the parser resolves tokens to NODES, not strings
This is the reframing the Epic makes possible. The parser is not a regex reading text; it is a step that **resolves filename tokens to existing graph nodes**. That is what makes the loop reinforcing: the graph teaches the parser, and the parser feeds the graph.
⚠️ **Never invent an entity from an unmatched token.** A misparse that creates a person is far more expensive to undo than one that leaves a field blank. An unresolved token is `unrecognised` and goes to a human.
### D4 — ⭐ NEW: a filename cannot say what a tag describes
Per the Epic's D3, a tag arriving with **no edge context** — which is exactly a bare token in a filename — is `unclassified` and forms **no edge**. It is recorded as a `pending_tag_association` naming the video it came from, and materialises into an edge only once the operator gives it a kind.
⚠️ **This is a behaviour change and it corrects an active defect.** Today the parser assigns every tag segment to the *video*, so an attribute term in a filename becomes a property of the wrong node. The graph is being mis-wired now, and every parsing run at scale makes more of it.
### D5 — ⭐ NEW: parsed values carry `filename` provenance and outrank nothing
Per the Epic's D7, a parsed value records origin `filename` — the lowest authority. It never overwrites a `download` or `operator` value, and it loses to a field of unknown provenance being filled by a download later. **Precedence stops being a matter of ordering and field semantics, and becomes a rule the code applies.**
### The grammar — four optional fields, and the app already generates it
```javascript
Performers  -  Series / Episode  -  Tags  -  Studio
```
Confirmed against the real 147 four-segment files. **Last** segment is a studio (top values ×18, ×8, ×6). **Third** is tags (×34, ×27, ×26, comma-joined). **Second** is near-unique per file (max ×3) — the signature of a title, not a category.
**Human Operator on which fields go missing:** *"It's usually the second segment that is missing, followed by the 4th. It's rare but not a defect when there are no tags."* So segment **count does not imply position**: a 3-segment name may be `Performers - Tags - Studio` or `Performers - Title - Tags`, and both are valid.
⭐ **The app already generates this exact convention.** `Asset.suggestedFileNameFromTags` joins `[actors, seriesTitleBlock, tags, studios]` with `' - '`, filtering empties. **The parser is the INVERSE of an existing function**, which yields the test that matters and is already written.
⚠️ **Generated names are lossy above 250 characters.** Fields drop in reverse priority — studio, then tags, then the series block — so a long-cast file may lack a studio *because it was dropped*, not because it was never known. **The parser must not read absence as evidence.**
### Disambiguating without a lexicon
Where no lexicon resolves a token, the corpus itself distinguishes the fields, needing no prior knowledge. **Quantified from the measured data** — count how often a token appears **in the same segment position** across the library:
| Occurrences | Read as | Measured basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **≥ 4** | categorical — a tag or a studio; **position decides which** | least-repeated studio observed was ×6; tags ×34, ×27, ×26 |
| **≤ 3** | a title | titles peaked at **×3** and are near-unique by nature |
`4` is a named constant, tuned against real data rather than fixed here — but it **has** a value and the boundary is exact: seen 3 times it is a title, seen 4 times it is categorical.
⚠️ **The heuristic never separates tag from studio.** It separates *categorical* from *title*; position does the rest. A rule attempting both would need a second threshold nothing in the data supports.
| Field | Signature |
| --- | --- |
| Tags | small, highly repeated set |
| Studio | repeated, larger set |
| Title | near-unique per file (max ×3) |
**Genuine ambiguity is skip-and-report** — a token matching both vocabularies is not resolvable by either signal.
**Human Operator on the fallback:** *"When they are completely ambiguous like this, we either: (least preferred) assume we don't have the studio (only tags), or (more preferred) skip and report to the user for manual resolution."*
### Small libraries decline the tool
**Human Operator:** *"Small libraries should not use this tool."* Below a corpus threshold nothing repeats, everything resembles a title, and every parse becomes a confident guess. **The tool declines and says why** — *"not enough files to tell tags from titles yet"* — rather than guessing and flagging low confidence.
💡 **The lexicon amendment softens this but does not remove it.** A small library with validated nodes can resolve by lexicon; a small library with neither lexicon nor corpus still declines. **Threshold: 50 assets.** Below 50 the corpus heuristic declines; at 50 or above it proceeds.
⭐ **A small library with a lexicon is not the same as a small library without one.** The threshold gates the **corpus heuristic**, not the whole tool. Below 50 assets the parser runs in **lexicon-only mode**: it resolves tokens that match validated nodes, skips and reports everything else, and never falls back to frequency counting. A library of ten files with confirmed studios still parses correctly; a library of ten files with nothing confirmed produces nothing, which is the honest result. Exact, so the boundary is testable — 49 declines, 50 runs — and a named constant, so tuning it is a one-line change rather than a hunt. **Not currently implemented.**
### Manual invocation only
**Human Operator:** *"Only trigger the bulk rename utility on manual invocation. Do not automatically rename files in bulk upon import."* Nothing renames and nothing bulk-parses as a side effect of importing.
**Human Operator, 2026-08-05:** *"I'd like to ensure the user has the opportunity to clean metadata and file names up manually before invoking a bulk update process."*
✅ **RESOLVED 2026-08-06 — answered by the Epic, not here.** This was left open pending the parser's real accuracy. *The Library Graph*'s **D9** and its test **T29** settle it: *"A file appearing after the migration arrives **`unreviewed`**, undeclared, unmatched and in the root, and proceeds through declaration, parsing, matching and relocation by the same code path."*
So a single new arrival **is** parsed, and specifically by the same path a legacy file takes — there is no separate import-time parser to design.
⚠️ **That does not contradict "manual invocation only" above.** The rule there is that nothing **bulk**-parses or bulk-renames as a side effect of importing. One arriving file going through the ordinary pipeline is not a bulk run, and D9's own framing — *"the migration is the steady-state process applied to a backlog"* — is that the two are the same code with different cardinality.

### ⚠️ D5's status, checked against the code 2026-08-06
**Edge Attributes phase 1 (migration v29) shipped ****`EdgeProvenance`** — `download` / `operator` / `filename` / `inferred`, carrying D7's precedence exactly as D5 requires. So the **vocabulary D5 asks for now exists and is tested.**
🚨 **But it is on EDGES, and the parser does not write edges.** `FileNameParser` produces values for `Asset` fields — `videoName`, the `studio:` and `actor:` tag strings — and **`Asset`**** has no per-field provenance at all** (verified by reading it: no provenance property, no map).
| D5 asks for | State |
| --- | --- |
| An origin vocabulary with precedence | ✅ built, v29 |
| Origin recorded on an **edge** the parser creates | ✅ possible now |
| Origin recorded on a **field value** the parser writes | ❌ does not exist |
⚠️ So D5 is **not** answered elsewhere in full. The half that matters most for this spec — *"a parsed value never overwrites a **`download`** or **`operator`** value"*, which is test **P2** — needs field-level provenance on `Asset`, and nothing has built it. The Epic's D7 specifies it as *one provenance map, not one property per field*; that remains unimplemented and is the real prerequisite for P2.
Until it exists, a parsed value can only be made safe the way the parser already is — by filling blanks and never overwriting — which is weaker than D5, because it cannot tell a blank that was never known from one a source will fill better tomorrow.
## Phase 2 — Generating names from the graph
### ⭐ D6 — AMENDED: renaming rides matching; the bulk run is a backstop
Per the Epic's D8, a video is relocated when its match is confirmed. **This changes Phase 2 from a campaign into a per-video consequence**, and the Epic's D9 makes it the same path a newly-added file takes.
What remains of the bulk utility is a **catch-up** over videos matched before this existed. Its requirements are unchanged and still mandatory: dry run first, resumable, reversible via old→new **full paths**, catalogue consistency.
### ⚠️ D7 — Collisions are the hard part, and they are common
Measured on the drive library **before** any parsing:
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Distinct names produced | 734 |
| Names claimed by more than one file | 88 |
| **Files that would collide** | **407 (19%)** |
| **Files with no identity metadata at all** | **1,048** |
Worst cases: one studio claims **53** files, another name **43**, a third **20**. Phase 1 reduces this — much of the missing metadata is in the filenames — but **cannot eliminate it**: a studio with fifty scenes and no other distinguishing metadata still yields fifty identical names.
**Decision: skip and report.** *"Humans need to engage to fix."* A file that cannot be named uniquely has not got enough metadata to be identified, and the honest response is to say so rather than manufacture a name.
💡 **Relocation-on-match improves this materially.** A file is named at the moment its metadata is richest — after a match supplied cast, studio and date — rather than from whatever the catalogue happened to hold during a batch. The 407 figure is a **pre-parse, pre-match** measurement and should be re-measured, not assumed.
### 🚫 A rejected option, recorded so it is not re-litigated
**Sequence suffixes** (`Name (2)`) were rejected as unstable: ordering decides who gets `(2)`, so a later run reshuffles. **Content-hash suffixes** (`Name [3f2b1c]`) are stable and deterministic and the fingerprints already exist — available per-run, but not the default, because a hash hides a metadata gap behind an identifier.
### Sequencing — video matching does NOT depend on the rename
A matcher queries with **graph** metadata — performers, studio, title — not with filenames. What it needs is a graph that knows things, which is **Phase 1**. Phase 1 therefore unblocks both the rename and the matching work; holding the spike behind a large migration would delay the answer for no benefit.
**Release dates do not gate this.** *"Do not wait on release dates"* — they are unobtainable from filenames (5 of 2,101) and come only from matching. Waiting would be cancelling. Under D6 the date is present by construction anyway, because the name is generated after the match.
## Test strategy (Constitution Art. III)
The Epic owns T18/T18b (path grammar and sanitisation), T23/T24 (move failure and reversibility), T28 (pending associations) and T5/T6 (tag kinds). The naming spec owns F1–F11. This spec adds:
- **P1 — Round-trip, for what the name actually carries.** `parse(suggestedFileNameFromTags(asset))` recovers every field the generated name **contains**. ⚠️ **For a name long enough to trigger truncation, the dropped fields cannot be recovered — they are not in the string.** The assertion is therefore that the surviving fields round-trip exactly **and that the dropped ones produce no proposal at all**: absence in a truncated name must never be read as evidence that the record lacks a studio, and must never clear or contradict a value the graph already holds.
- **P2 — A parsed value never overwrites a populated field**, and never a `download` or `operator` value regardless of arrival order.
- **P3 — Actors and tags union; nothing curated is lost.**
- **P4 — An unmatched token creates no entity.** Asserted against a store that fails the test if any node is created.
- **P5 — Parsing is idempotent.** A second run changes nothing.
- **P6 — The lexicon overrules position.** A token in the studio position that resolves to a validated *performer* node is read as a performer, and the row is raised for review rather than silently overruled.
- **P7 — Position still works with no lexicon.** Against an empty graph, every observed segment shape parses to the expected fields, including the 4-segment case.
- **P8 — A parsed tag never reaches a video as an edge.** It becomes an `unclassified` node and a pending association naming the source video. Asserted against the write boundary, which must reject the edge outright.
- **P9 — A small library declines.** Below the threshold the tool refuses with a reason and produces no proposals — asserted by the absence of output, not by a low confidence score.
- **P10 — Collisions are detected before any write, never during one.**
- **P11 — Nothing runs unattended.** Neither parsing nor renaming is triggered by a scan or an import.
- **P12 — The catch-up dry run writes nothing.** It produces a complete plan — every intended old and new **full path** — and mutates neither the filesystem nor the catalogue. Asserted by comparing a full filesystem and database snapshot before and after.
- **P13 — The catch-up run is resumable.** Killed midway and restarted, it completes the remaining files and re-does none. Every file is either fully relocated with its catalogue row consistent, or untouched — never half.
- **P14 — The catch-up run is reversible.** Replaying the recorded old→new full-path mapping restores the original layout exactly, including files whose directories the run created.
- **P16 — Failure states are exercised, not assumed.** P10–P15 are asserted against doubles that inject: a permission-denied write, a disk-full write, a database failure mid-transaction, and a process kill between the filesystem move and the catalogue update — the last being the specific window in which a file and its record can disagree. In every case the library is left consistent and the failure is reported. A test suite that only exercises success has not tested a migration at all.
- **P17 — Ambiguity is reported, never resolved.** A token resolving to several node types, a segment count outside the grammar, and a sub-threshold corpus each produce a report entry and zero proposals.
- **P15 — A rollback restores the catalogue too.** After reversal, every asset's `relativePath` matches where its file actually is, and no fingerprint, thumbnail or contact sheet has been orphaned — the failure mode that makes a rename dangerous in the first place.
## Evidence
Measured 2026-08-04 against the external-drive library: 2,101 assets, 1,172 with no actor tag, 1,154 of those with descriptive filenames, 407 colliding under the scene grammar, 1,048 with no identity metadata. Segment-shape counts measured 2026-08-03. Related: *The Library Graph* (D3, D5, D7, D8, D9), *File Naming & Metadata Storage Strategy*.
